chapter_theme: Sayambavai is dressed, guarded and walks in procession to the swayamvara hall, her women praise her, and a herald names the assembled kings to her one by one, praising each by line, deeds, appearance and country, and twice by the merit or austerity that wins his embrace.

1794.reading: The king's daughter, in her jewelled upper room, is told something about the lord ladies' grace and steps down from her flowered seat above the golden couch.
1794.nuance: The verse names no one; 'the king's daughter' is taken as Sayambavai because this is the swayamvara sarukkam. Line 3 is hard to construe and carries the editor's mark (கு) on line 2.
1794.event: Sayambavai rises from her couch in the palace and steps down from her seat, to go out to the wedding hall.

1795.reading: Women like creepers bind the jewelled girdle on her, tie up her hair, tighten her bodices and close around the peacock-like girl with spears in their hands.
1795.nuance: The spears carried by her attendants make the bride's procession a guarded one, as the armed maidens of 862-975 are.
1795.event: The maidens of her guard dress Sayambavai and surround her with spears.

1796.reading: With her companions and nurses she goes through the courts, the girl who rules the hearts of kings, like the moon moving among stars and reflected in the clear jewelled waters.
1796.nuance: The moon-and-stars simile gives her the kings' longing before any king is shown.
1796.event: Sayambavai walks with her retinue towards the hall.

1797.reading: As she walks, bees follow her, the minds of the kings follow, the eyes of onlookers delight, and the praise and music of the eight quarters follow, and she steps gently over fallen petals.
1797.event: Sayambavai walks on among following bees, kings' thoughts and the sounds of praise.

1798.reading: Her soft feet ache, the kings' thoughts throb, their desire swells and she enters the gem-set mansion, dark and bright as a flower.
1798.nuance: Line 1 is hard: 'சராவி' is a rare or damaged word, so the cause of the pain in the soft feet is not fixed.
1798.event: Sayambavai reaches the jewelled mansion where the kings are seated.

1799.reading: Her women cry 'honour, honour' to her as gold, as a gem-branch, as the lamp of the kings' line, and beg her to step slowly on the soft flowers lest her fine waist hurt, as she enters the hall.
1799.event: Her attendants praise her and warn her to tread softly as she goes into the hall.

1800.reading: At the shining steps her attendants salute her, and in the moonlit court of the mansion, when the screen-women draw back, she appears blazing before the kings, whose minds waver.
1800.nuance: Line 3 (கணிதயங்கு வினைநவின்ற ... திரைமகளிர்) is hard to construe; I read it as women who hold a screen and remove it.
1800.event: Sayambavai appears before the assembled kings and they are shaken.

1801.reading: A man with a gold-bound cane, who shows the kings in order and speaks softly to the girl, begins to name them.
1801.nuance: The verse does not give the speaker's office; 'herald' is my label for the man who names the kings, as the speakers of 1802-1816 do.
1801.event: The herald points out the kings to Sayambavai one by one and begins to speak to her.

1802.reading: He points to the first king, broad-chested and scented with the sandal that the women's breasts touch, who sits on a lion seat, the lord of the Ikshvaku line with no peer here.
1802.event: The herald points Sayambavai to the king of the Ikshvaku line.

1803.reading: The herald says this king is descended from one who bore the wheel of grace of the First Lord and was crowned by the one who burned the harmful karmas, and asks who among kings could match his strength.
1803.nuance: The praise runs through the king's descent from the First Lord and his line, not through any deed of his own; the Jain colouring of 'அருளாழி' and 'காதி' is the poet's, but the verse makes no doctrinal claim.

1804.reading: He mounted a single wheel-chariot, drove it across the middle of the sea, seized the gods' gold chariots and crowns and jewels as tribute, and kept the whole world under one umbrella, so that after Bharata the earth lost her sorrow.
1804.nuance: Bharata is the measure: the earth's relief 'after Bharata' is set on this king, as 397 sets Bharata's rule on the First Lord's grace.

1805.reading: Skipping his lineage, youth and looks, the herald tells the king's daughter to hear of the king beside him, seated on a gem couch at his left, the lord of the Kuru line.
1805.event: The herald moves on to the king of the Kuru line seated beside the first.

1806.reading: By the grace of the lord of dharma, the herald says, the wheel-holder removed the world's sorrow; kings bow their crowns to him like servants, and he is the foremost in his line.
1806.nuance: 'அறவரசன்' may name the Jain teacher or a king; the verse does not say. Whether 1806-1807 praise the Kuru king of 1805 or begin another is not fixed by the text.

claims.claim: the world's sorrow was ended by the grace of the lord of dharma

1807.reading: He bore the rain of weapons poured by the gods' sea-host, and met the arrow-tower, and bees and women's dark eyes never leave his chest; his greatness, says the herald, needs no telling.

1808.reading: At his left side another king sits on a gem couch, fanned by white fly-whisks, his chest red with kunkuma and as broad as a red mountain, and the herald asks her to hear of him too.
1808.event: The herald points Sayambavai to the next king seated beside him.

1809.reading: When the First Lord stood in the sandal grove as a king of renunciation, one played the harp, won a boon and ruled the world on the northern mountain, and this king is the descendant praised by the gods.
1809.nuance: The harp-playing boon-winner on the northern mountain matches the story of Nami told at 538-547; 'சயம்பூறான்' (line 1) is not a word I can read, so the identification is not fixed.

1810.reading: This young king, spear shining, comes of the Ugra line which the wheel-kings founded and which held the sea-bound earth, and the herald tells the king's chief daughter that he will name a few more.
1810.event: The herald points to the young Ugra-line king and promises to name a few more.

1811.reading: The herald points to the lord of Kundalam, whose line lights the lord of the world's house, a spear-armed youth, and says there is no king like him here.
1811.nuance: 'நாதவன்' and 'குண்டலத்தார்' may be names of line and place or epithets; the verse does not fix them.
1811.event: The herald points to the lord of Kundalam.

1812.reading: The herald names the lord of the Surya garland, a lion of the Hari line, and says that the women who have not embraced his broad chest have not met merit.
1812.nuance: Line 4 can be read with the women as those who have not embraced him, or those who have not 'united' with merit (புண்ணியங்கள்); I give both as one claim. The herald is selling a suitor, so the claim is his own.
1812.event: The herald points to the king of the Surya garland of the Hari line.

claims.claim: embracing this king's chest is the fruit of merit won earlier

1813.reading: The herald points to the lord of the rich land around Madurai, where white conches and pearls mingle in the sea, sugarcane grows thick, waterfalls hang and elephants sleep to the women's lutes in the groves.
1813.event: The herald points to the lord of the Madurai country.

1814.reading: The herald says that this king under a tall umbrella, with elephants like thundering clouds, is a descendant of the moon-line, with the sandal of the southern hills on his chest, a tilaka on the brow of the world.
1814.nuance: The moon-line, the southern hill and the Madurai verse before suggest the Pandya, but the verse does not name him.
1814.event: The herald points to the king under the tall umbrella of the moon-line.

1815.reading: The herald names the lord of Karapuram of the sun-line, a bright-spear youth in a land of sugarcane and creeper, and says the women who have won his garlanded chest had done austerity.
1815.nuance: 'தவஞ்செய்தாரே' makes past austerity the cause of present good fortune, as 1812 does with merit; the herald uses a doctrine of former deeds as part of the king's praise.
1815.event: The herald points to the lord of Karapuram of the sun-line.

claims.claim: winning this king's embrace is the fruit of austerity done earlier

1816.reading: The herald points to the lord of Urandai, in whose city swans play and young women walk, and says he keeps a war-drum, a banner wall, cool water, machines and flowers, and three ghats in each of three kinds.
1816.nuance: Lines 3-4 list the king's possessions in threes; I cannot fix what each three is.
1816.event: The herald points to the king of Urandai.

links.note: 1797 sets her procession to the sounds of praise and music from all quarters; Naladiyar 23 shows wedding drums in a hall turning to funeral drums for the groom.
links.teaches: The poem fills the bridal march with music and hope, and the quatrain says the same drums can announce the end of the groom.

gains.a: The procession gains the shadow that its music may not last, which the poem leaves out here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a wedding at its brightest, before any reversal, which is the moment it warns against trusting.

links.note: 1798 shows kings' desire swelling as she enters; Naladiyar 17 tells the man not to desire a spear-eyed girl, who will stoop on a staff.
links.teaches: The poem lets the reader see her with the kings' eyes, and the quatrain supplies what those eyes will not see.

gains.a: The kings' longing gains a limit set by age, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a young woman actually seen, so its warning is tested against an entrance that wins every eye.

links.note: 1804 sets this king's glory 'after Bharata'; 397 says the First Lord's grace made a king of the earth Bharata.
links.teaches: The herald's yardstick, Bharata, is the ruler the earlier verse shows as the First Lord's gift, so the king's glory is measured against a grace-given one.

links.note: 1809 gives the harp-playing boon-winner of the northern mountain; 543 has Dharanan come at Nami's song, which is how the boon was won.
links.teaches: What the herald says in two lines is the story told at length at 538-547, so the hall's praise draws on the book's own earlier telling.

links.note: 1810 praises a king for the line that bred him; Naladiyar 195 says a lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort, not by name.
links.teaches: The herald's whole mode of praise is descent, and the quatrain offers another test for the same kings, what each has done.

gains.a: The suitor's praise gains a test the herald does not apply, effort and learning in the man himself.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall of kings praised for birth, which shows how common the claim it denies was.

links.note: 1815 says women who reached this king's chest had done austerity; Naladiyar 31 says present comfort comes from earlier austerity and is lost without more.
links.teaches: The herald's line puts a marriage on the same ledger of past austerity that the quatrain keeps, and the quatrain adds that it runs out.

gains.a: The praise gains a warning that earlier austerity wears down, which the herald omits.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a new case, a bride's good fortune, where its past austerity pays out in a marriage rather than a house.

links.note: 1814 puts a moon-line king under a tall umbrella with cloud-like elephants; Purananuru 3 puts the Pandya under a white umbrella like the full moon.
links.teaches: The poem makes the moon-line king's umbrella the sign of his kind, as the Sangam poem does for the Pandya, so the herald's king reads as the Pandya of that tradition.

gains.a: The verse gains a Sangam picture that fills in the umbrella and moon that it names only in passing.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a late epic that keeps its image but brings it to a marriage hall, not a battlefield.

links.note: 1816 places a king at Urandai among swans, drums and banners; Akananuru 385 uses Uranthai as the standard of a house rich in festival.
links.teaches: Urandai is the name of wealth in both books, so the herald's list of its splendours carries a meaning already known from the Sangam poem.

gains.a: The epic city gains an earlier use of its name as a measure of richness.
gains.b: The Akam poem gains a king's side of the city, whose wealth it uses only as a comparison.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, whose swayamvara this is
the armed maidens who guard Sayambavai
the attendant women who praise her as she goes in
the man with the gold-bound cane who names the kings to Sayambavai; his office is not named in the verses

source_issues: 1799-1816 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1794 line 2 carries the editor's mark (கு) and lines 2-3 are hard to construe.
1798 line 1 (சராவி), 1800 line 3 (திரைமகளிர்) and 1809 line 1 (சயம்பூறான்) are rare or damaged words.
1806 line 5 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed by the build.
